rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Gravitational potential $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ is the work per unit mass to bring a test mass from infinity; potential energy $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ is the negative binding energy of two masses. Near the surface $U \approx mgh$. The field relates to the potential by $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$, and circular orbits have total energy $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, confirming their bound nature.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Gravitational potential: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ (J/kg)
Gravitational potential energy: $U = mV = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ (J)
Near the surface: $U = mgh$ ($h \ll R$)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Field vs Potential Distinction:** Gravitational field $\vec{g} = -GM/r^2 \, \hat{r}$ is a *vector* (force per unit mass). Gravitational potential $V = -GM/r$ is a *scalar* (work per unit mass). The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $\vec{g} = -\nabla V = -dV/dr \, \hat{r}$.  ·  **Equipotential Surfaces:** Surfaces of constant $V$. For a point mass, they are concentric spheres. No work is done moving a test mass along an equipotential; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Both V and U are defined with reference zero at infinity — that is why they are negative.  ·  Use $U = mgh$ only for small heights ($h \ll R$); use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for space-scale problems.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: V at Earth's surface: $V = -\frac{GM}{R} = -6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J/kg}$.  ·  U of 1000 kg satellite at $r = 6.8\times 10^{6} \text{ m}$: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r} = -5.9\times 10^{10} \text{ J}$.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$ (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.  ·  ❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive $V$ and $U$ starting from $F = \frac{GMm}{r^2}$ by integration.  ·  Solve 5 numericals for V and U at various distances.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Escape-energy shortcut: energy to infinity = $GMm/R = mgR$ (since $g = \frac{GM}{R^2}$).  ·  Orbital energy memory: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = U/2$ means $K = -U/2$.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Calculate the gravitational potential at a point $3\times 10^{7} \text{ m}$ from the centre of Earth ($M = 6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$).  ·  Find the gravitational potential energy of a 1500 kg satellite at an altitude of 2000 km above Earth.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Derivation of $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ from integrating $F = \frac{GMm}{r^2}$ is a standard question.  ·  Numericals on satellite total energy and escape energy are frequently asked.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Gravitational potential $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ is scalar work per unit mass.  ·  Gravitational potential energy $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ equals the negative binding energy.  ·  Near the surface $U = mgh$; far away use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$.  ·  $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ links the vector field to the scalar potential.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ is negative, approaching zero at infinity.  ·  $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ is the energy of the (bound) system, negative for attraction.  ·  Near Earth's surface $U = mgh$ is the appropriate approximation.  ·  Potential and field connect: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Gravitational potential energy is exactly the 'missing' energy that binds systems — this is why the binding energy of Earth + satellite equals $|U|$.  ·  The concept of potential is useful because it is scalar: complex many-body problems reduce to addition rather than vector resolution.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: How much energy is required to move a 3000 kg spacecraft from Earth's surface to infinity?  ·  A 700 kg probe is moved from $r = 8\times 10^{6} \text{ m}$ to $r = 5\times 10^{6} \text{ m}$. Find the change in its potential energy.  ·  Derive that for a circular orbit $v^2 = \frac{GM}{r}$ and hence $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Conceptual MCQ: why is potential energy negative? → because zero is at infinity and gravity is attractive.  ·  Linking $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ to a $V$–$r$ graph slope appears in higher-level questions.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Escape energy per kg: $GM/R = 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 17 \text{ kWh}$ per kg.  ·  Near surface: a 2 kg mass lifted 10 m gains $U = mgh = 196 \text{ J}$.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The gravitational potential at a point at distance r from mass M is: → B  ·  Gravitational potential energy of two masses m and M at distance r is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$. At infinity $V = 0$, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.  ·  **Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply $GMm/r$ of energy to separate the masses to infinity.  ·  **Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — its total mechanical energy is $E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Circular orbits are bound: $E_{\text{total}} = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = U/2$.  ·  Field from potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$  ·  Total orbital energy: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = U/2$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Superposition Advantage:** Potentials add as scalars ($V_{total} = \sum V_i$), which is simpler than adding field vectors. This makes potential calculations easier for multiple mass distributions, especially when symmetry is broken.  ·  Total energy of a circular orbit is negative: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$.  ·  ❌ '$U = mgh$ and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: $mgh$ is the CHANGE in $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface ($-\frac{GM}{R}$) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.  ·  ❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes $-\frac{GMm}{2r}$ (less negative).  ·  ❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but $U \approx 0$). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Total energy of circular orbit: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ — negative, so the orbit is bound.  ·  Potential is a scalar — use scalar addition with multiple masses.  ·  The escape energy equals $|U|$ at the surface: $GMm/R$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB may ask 'derive $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ starting from $F = \frac{GMm}{r^2}$' — know the integration step.  ·  $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ (potential) and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ (potential energy) both take zero at infinity — hence negative for attracted masses.  ·  Near Earth's surface use $U = mgh$; for space-scale distances use the inverse-r form.
